findings.source_passage: Do I look the sort of girl that's always falling in love with every man she meets? / You do not. You look the sort of girl that's mighty often getting fallen in love with!
findings.source_locator: exchange between Tuppence and Julius in the car, before the marriage proposal
findings.why_it_matters: This sharp comic exchange is characteristic Christie banter, establishes Julius's flattery mode, and sets up the proposal; its absence flattens the tonal pivot from gloom to courtship and removes a small but distinctively voiced beat.
findings.suggested_fix: Reinsert the two-line exchange verbatim or near-verbatim before Julius pivots to asking about marriage views.

findings.source_passage: I suppose I shall sleep with his photograph under my pillow, and dream about him all night. It's dreadful to feel you've been false to your principles.
findings.source_locator: Tuppence's soliloquy at the dressing-table, after crying over Tommy's photo
findings.why_it_matters: This self-mocking interior monologue is the voice-defining passage of the segment; its dry irony ('false to your principles') characterises Tuppence's self-aware romanticism and is the emotional and tonal centrepiece of her reflection. Without it the soliloquy loses its satirical register and becomes merely sentimental.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the 'photograph under my pillow' / 'false to your principles' passage and the preceding 'backsliding' line verbatim or close to it in Tuppence's interior monologue.

findings.source_passage: You'll be darned lonesome, you poor kid. / I shall be all right, snapped Tuppence with her usual resentment of any kind of pity.
findings.source_locator: Julius and Tuppence exchange just before 'What about marriage?'
findings.why_it_matters: The beat captures Tuppence's characteristic bristling at sympathy and Julius's warmth; its absence makes the marriage proposal feel abrupt and slightly unmotivated.
findings.suggested_fix: Add the 'darned lonesome / I shall be all right' exchange in a single sentence before the marriage-views question.

summary: The draft is broadly faithful but drops two voice-defining passages—the 'fallen in love with' repartee and Tuppence's ironic 'false to your principles' self-reproach—reducing the segment's characteristic comic-ironic register to a flatter emotional tone; no high-severity losses are present.
